units.quote: 29 CFR 825.110 — Eligible employee.
units.meaning: This is the title of the regulation designating that the section establishes the criteria and rules for determining who constitutes an eligible employee under the FMLA, providing structural context without imposing substantive legal obligations on its own.

units.quote: (1) Has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months, and
scope_quotes: (a) An eligible employee is an employee of a covered employer who:
units.meaning: To qualify as an eligible employee of a covered employer under the FMLA, an employee must have been employed by that employer for a minimum threshold of at least 12 months.

units.quote: (2) Has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave ( see § 825.801 for special hours of service requirements for airline flight crew employees), and
scope_quotes: (a) An eligible employee is an employee of a covered employer who:
units.meaning: To qualify as an eligible employee, an employee must have been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the date leave begins, subject to special hours of service rules for airline flight crew employees under § 825.801.

units.quote: (3) Is employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite. See § 825.105(b) regarding employees who work outside the U.S.
scope_quotes: (a) An eligible employee is an employee of a covered employer who:
units.meaning: To qualify as an eligible employee, an employee must be employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within a 75-mile radius of that worksite, taking into account § 825.105(b) for employees working outside the United States.

units.quote: (b) The 12 months an employee must have been employed by the employer need not be consecutive months, provided
units.meaning: The 12 months of employment required to establish FMLA eligibility are not required to be consecutive months, subject to the break-in-service conditions that follow.

units.quote: (1) Subject to the exceptions provided in paragraph (b)(2) of this section, employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.
scope_quotes: (b) The 12 months an employee must have been employed by the employer need not be consecutive months, provided
units.meaning: Unless one of the exceptions in paragraph (b)(2) applies, an employer is exempt from any requirement to count periods of employment that occurred prior to a break in service lasting seven years or more when determining if the employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.

units.quote: (i) The employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of his or her Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), 38 U.S.C. 4301, et seq., covered service obligation. The period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must be also counted in determining whether the employee has been employed for at least 12 months by the employer.
scope_quotes: (2) Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where:
units.meaning: As an exception to the seven-year break rule, an employer must count prior employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years if the break was caused by the employee fulfilling a USERRA-covered service obligation, and the period of absence from work necessitated by or due to that USERRA service must also be counted toward the 12-month requirement.

units.quote: However, this section does not provide any greater entitlement to the employee than would be available under the USERRA; or
scope_quotes: (2) Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where:

(i) The employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of his or her Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), 38 U.S.C. 4301, et seq., covered service obligation.
units.meaning: The crediting of USERRA service breaks does not confer any greater legal entitlement on the employee than what would otherwise be available under USERRA itself.

units.quote: (ii) A written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (e.g., for purposes of the employee furthering his or her education or for childrearing purposes).
scope_quotes: (2) Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where:
units.meaning: As an exception to the seven-year break rule, an employer must count prior employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years if a written agreement (including a collective bargaining agreement) exists reflecting the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break (such as for education or childrearing).

units.quote: (3) If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (sick, vacation) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (e.g., workers' compensation, group health plan benefits, etc.), the week counts as a week of employment.
units.meaning: Any week during which an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of the week—including periods of paid or unpaid leave like sick leave or vacation where other compensation or benefits like workers' compensation or group health plan benefits are provided—legally counts as a full week of employment.

units.quote: For purposes of determining whether intermittent/occasional/casual employment qualifies as at least 12 months, 52 weeks is deemed to be equal to 12 months.
units.meaning: When assessing whether intermittent, occasional, or casual employment satisfies the 12-month employment threshold, 52 weeks of employment is defined and deemed to be equivalent to 12 months.

units.quote: (4) Nothing in this section prevents employers from considering employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.
units.meaning: Employers are permitted, at their discretion, to count and consider an employee's employment preceding a continuous break in service of more than seven years toward the 12-month requirement.

units.quote: However, if an employer chooses to recognize such prior employment, the employer must do so uniformly, with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.
scope_quotes: (4) Nothing in this section prevents employers from considering employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.
units.meaning: If an employer elects to recognize prior employment before a continuous break of more than seven years, the employer must apply that policy uniformly to all employees who have similar breaks in service.

units.quote: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work. See 29 CFR part 785.
units.meaning: Unless governed by paragraph (c)(2) or the airline flight crew rules in § 825.801, the determination of whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service must follow FLSA principles for determining compensable hours of work as outlined in 29 CFR part 785.

units.quote: The determining factor is the number of hours an employee has worked for the employer within the meaning of the FLSA.
scope_quotes: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work.
units.meaning: The critical and determinative factor for meeting the hours requirement is the actual number of hours the employee has worked for the employer within the statutory meaning of the FLSA.

units.quote: The determination is not limited by methods of recordkeeping, or by compensation agreements that do not accurately reflect all of the hours an employee has worked for or been in service to the employer.
scope_quotes: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work.
units.meaning: Calculating hours worked is not restricted or constrained by employer recordkeeping techniques or by compensation agreements that fail to accurately capture all hours an employee actually worked or remained in service.

units.quote: Any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA's principles may be used.
scope_quotes: (c)(1) Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section and in § 825.801 containing the special hours of service requirement for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to the principles established under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) for determining compensable hours of work.
units.meaning: Parties are permitted to use any accurate accounting of actual hours worked, provided it conforms to FLSA principles.

units.quote: (2) An employee returning from USERRA-covered service shall be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service in determining the employee's eligibility for FMLA-qualifying leave.
units.meaning: An employer must credit an employee returning from USERRA-covered service with the hours of service that the employee would have performed but for the absence necessitated by or due to that USERRA service, when evaluating FMLA leave eligibility.

units.quote: Accordingly, a person reemployed following USERRA-covered service has the hours that would have been worked for the employer added to any hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period to meet the hours of service requirement.
scope_quotes: (2) An employee returning from USERRA-covered service shall be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service in determining the employee's eligibility for FMLA-qualifying leave.
units.meaning: A person reemployed after USERRA-covered service must have the hypothetical hours they would have worked added to their actually worked hours during the preceding 12-month period to satisfy the 1,250 hours of service requirement.

units.quote: In order to determine the hours that would have been worked during the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service, the employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used for calculations. See § 825.801(c) for special rules applicable to airline flight crew employees.
scope_quotes: (2) An employee returning from USERRA-covered service shall be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service in determining the employee's eligibility for FMLA-qualifying leave.
units.meaning: To compute unworked hours during a USERRA absence, an employee's pre-service work schedule can generally be used as the calculation basis, subject to special airline flight crew rules in § 825.801(c).

units.quote: (3) In the event an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee, including for employees who are exempt from FLSA's requirement that a record be kept of their hours worked (e.g., bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees as defined in FLSA Regulations, 29 CFR part 541), the employer has the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite hours.
units.meaning: If an employer fails to maintain accurate records of hours worked—including for FLSA-exempt executive, administrative, and professional employees under 29 CFR part 541—the legal burden of proof falls on the employer to show that the employee did not work the required 1,250 hours.

units.quote: An employer must be able to clearly demonstrate, for example, that full-time teachers ( see § 825.102 for definition) of an elementary or secondary school system, or institution of higher education, or other educational establishment or institution (who often work outside the classroom or at their homes) did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months in order to claim that the teachers are not eligible for FMLA leave. See § 825.801(d) for special rules applicable to airline flight crew employees.
scope_quotes: (3) In the event an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee, including for employees who are exempt from FLSA's requirement that a record be kept of their hours worked (e.g., bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees as defined in FLSA Regulations, 29 CFR part 541), the employer has the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite hours.
units.meaning: To substantiate a claim that full-time teachers (as defined in § 825.102) of educational institutions are not FMLA eligible, an employer must clearly demonstrate that the teachers did not work 1,250 hours in the previous 12 months, accounting for out-of-classroom or home work (subject to § 825.801(d) for airline flight crew).

units.quote: (d) The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has been employed by the employer for a total of at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.
units.meaning: An employer must determine whether an employee satisfies both the 12 months of employment requirement and the 1,250 hours of service requirement specifically as of the date the requested FMLA leave is scheduled to begin.

units.quote: An employee may be on non-FMLA leave at the time he or she meets the 12-month eligibility requirement, and in that event, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after the employee meets the eligibility requirement would be FMLA leave. See § 825.300(b) for rules governing the content of the eligibility notice given to employees.
scope_quotes: (d) The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has been employed by the employer for a total of at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.
units.meaning: An employee is permitted to be on non-FMLA leave when reaching the 12-month eligibility threshold, and once the threshold is satisfied, any subsequent portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason constitutes FMLA leave (referencing notice content rules in § 825.300(b)).

units.quote: (e) Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to ascertain an employee's eligibility for FMLA benefits is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.
units.meaning: The determination of whether 50 or more employees work within 75 miles of the worksite must be assessed at the specific time the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

units.quote: Whether the leave is to be taken at one time or on an intermittent or reduced leave schedule basis, once an employee is determined eligible in response to that notice of the need for leave, the employee's eligibility is not affected by any subsequent change in the number of employees employed at or within 75 miles of the employee's worksite, for that specific notice of the need for leave.
scope_quotes: (e) Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to ascertain an employee's eligibility for FMLA benefits is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.
units.meaning: Once an employee is determined eligible based on notice of leave (regardless of whether the leave is continuous, intermittent, or on a reduced schedule), that eligibility is locked for that notice and cannot be altered by later fluctuations in the headcount within 75 miles.

units.quote: Similarly, an employer may not terminate employee leave that has already started if the employee count drops below 50.
scope_quotes: (e) Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to ascertain an employee's eligibility for FMLA benefits is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.
units.meaning: An employer is prohibited from terminating an employee's leave that has already commenced if the total number of employees drops below 50.

units.quote: For example, if an employer employs 60 employees in August, but expects that the number of employees will drop to 40 in December, the employer must grant FMLA benefits to an otherwise eligible employee who gives notice of the need for leave in August for a period of leave to begin in December.
scope_quotes: (e) Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to ascertain an employee's eligibility for FMLA benefits is determined when the employee gives notice of the need for leave.
units.meaning: An employer is legally required to grant FMLA benefits to an otherwise eligible employee who gives notice of need for leave while the 50-employee/75-mile threshold is met (e.g., 60 in August), even if the employee count is anticipated to drop below 50 by the time leave begins (e.g., 40 in December).
